I know in the US and (at least) in many places in Europe, it is customary to flush the toilet paper after use. However in here we don't do this. We usually have a separated trash can (many times with a pedal-operated lid) that is used only for bathroom trash, including toilet paper (more things include dental floss, cotton balls and swabs, etc..), and it usually sits right next to the toilet.

I never figured why we don't flush toilet paper, but I guess it has to do with keeping the most solids as possible from the sewer (making treatment less expensive, maybe?).
It could also be a plumbing issue to avoid clogging the pipes. Some TPs are thicker and absorb a lot of liquid, so they get stuck and cause backups, overflowing, flooding, and stuff...

I noticed that voat is using a SSL cert from StartCom. If you stay in their free tier, that may work for you. However, if you want a wildcard cert, I would recommend going to http://www.garrisonhost.com/ssl-certificates/alphassl.html

GlobalSign's AlphaSSL has full browser and mobile support, so there's no reason not to go with it since it is the cheapest.

I'm currently using https://sslmate.com because it's ridiculously easy to use and pretty cheap.

I can't wait for https://letsencrypt.org/ to go-live, it is equally easy, free, and I like it for ideological reasons. It won't have wildcards to begin with, but shouldn't be a big deal since it's free anyway :)

Interesting article, thanks for sharing! I very much agree with Ben Jones' excerpt, especially:

Perceptions of the flag depend upon context. At a national cemetery or national battlefield it is seen in the historical context of the American Civil War. At popular re-enactments of that war’s events, or in films like “Gettysburg” or “Gone With the Wind”, it is seen in a theatrical context. In the television series “The Dukes of Hazzard” the flag on top of Duke boys car has been seen as a symbol of a non-racist Southern spirit by millions of viewers internationally.

Personally, whenever I see the Confederate flag I feel a sense of pride that I associate with the South. It reminds me of pecans, peaches, Southern Belles, humid summers, courteous people, and so much more. It reminds me of the family trips we'd take every summer, driving from the South Atlanta Metro area to Daytona Beach, and passing these flags which were flying in so many people's front yards, sometimes above the produce stands they'd set up to attract travelers. You better bet we stopped and picked up some Vidalia onions and boiled peanuts along the way.

However, I know there's a stigma associated with this flag, than anyone who openly flies it is racist. Even though this is a generalization I have never spoken aloud how I feel about the Confederate flag, in fear that I'll be labeled a racist, until now.
To me, it's a symbol of treason against the Constitution, and I don't understand why a bunch of white-supremacist traitors should be celebrated, even if they are somebodies great-great-grandparents.
